messages.subject: Re: Moderation, moderated mediation
messages.subject_clean: Moderation, moderated mediation
messages.body_plain:
Dear Dr.,
Thanks for the reply. As an  enthusiastic rookie, I immediately started to work on semtools: inprod function. First of all, I'm trying to fit the Sem models in lavaan, after that I conduct a non-informative Bayesian Sem and try to catch the similar results, and mostly I do. Inprod's residual centering gave the best results for my demo.

I don't want to take your time but I'd be appreciated if you may have a quick look at the codes. In here all variables are first-order latent variables and I'm trying to observe this moderated mediation sem. (Cid variable is the moderator, and Kac is the dependent one; you may see on the pic.). I just put the necessary ones not to busy you, and this model works good for both lavaan & blavaan.

The plotprobe command gives the simple slope clearly in lavaan, I just wanted to try it out for blavaan and it gives the same graph, but a little broken =)
As you said, that would be great if you may add this feature in the next update, so blavaan 'll be ready for moderations  ! thanks in advance !

Gokay

messages.subject: Difference between BRMSEA and RMSEA (in bivariate latent change score model)
messages.subject_clean: Difference between BRMSEA and RMSEA (in bivariate latent change score model)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I am trying to estimate a bivariate latent change score model that also includes using the change scores as predictors of an outcome. The model converges fine. When comparing the ML estimates and Bayesian posterior means, they are extremely similar.

However, in my model, I have noticed that the estimated (posterior mean) BRMSEA is quite different from the maximum likelihood estimate (.15 instead of .07). This is specific to the BRMSEA and not the same for, eg. BCFI, - there, results are very similiar to the frequentist estimates.

When trying out different models using other data, it also seemed that the BRMSEA is especially sensitive.
How should one deal with such results? I know that the overall posterior is more important than the mean, but for the BRMSEA it seems like the entire distribution is very far from the ML point estimate. Is it because of the type of model used (df=16, N=350)?
Any help or ideas are greatly appreciated!
best
Mischa

messages.subject: Re: Longitudinal Measurement Invariance
messages.subject_clean: Longitudinal Measurement Invariance
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dr. Garnier-Villarreal and Dr.Merkle,

Thank you very much for your help with my previous questions!

I encountered more issues while testing the approximate invariance with ordered categorical items.

To reduce the computation time, I treated the longitudinal measurement invariance test question as a multi-group one and converted the data into a long format. I used the Lavan default method for model identification and the models converged with the WLSMV estimator. Specifically,

1. Configural model: freely estimates loadings and thresholds in all groups, and constrains the latent item responses as variances of 1 and intercepts of 0 in all groups. The common-factor variances are set to 1 and means are set to 0 in all groups.
2. Loadings invariance model: constrained the loadings to be equal across groups, thresholds freely estimated in all groups. The latent item responses were constrained with variances of 1 and intercepts of 0. The common-factor variances were constrained to 1 in the first group and freely estimated in other groups, and the common-factor means were constrained to 0 in all groups.
3. Thresholds invariance model: constrained the loadings and thresholds to be equal across groups. The latent item variances were fixed to 1 in the first group and freely estimated in other groups. The common-factor mean and variance were fixed to 0 and 1 in the first group and freely estimated in other groups.

To test loading approximate invariance, I added the labels of item loadings in the wiggle statement, and the models converged with different data I simulated.
However, when I further tested the loading exact invariance + thresholds, approximate invariance model, by adding the thresholds labels into the wiggle statements, the models failed to converge.
Similarly, when testing the loadings + thresholds approximate invariance model, the models failed to converge. Moreover, some of the models had an error message: Error in validate_ll(x) : All input values must be finite.

I understand that treating longitudinal data as multi-group data introduces a definite source of model misspecification that may cause the convergence issue. However, I tried testing the thresholds approximate invariance model using the wide format data, but I still have the convergence issue with the thresholds approximate invariance model and loading + thresholds approximate invariance model.

Do you have any suggestions on correctly testing the thresholds approximate invariance with ordered categorical indicators? e.g. specific model identification methods, increase the burin-in sample, or increase/decrease the wiggle sd?

 I attached the syntax and data for your reference. Thank you very much!

Hi Ed,
thanks for getting back to me so quickly!

Here's the model code and the sessionInfo() output:

bivariate_lcs_model <-'
#Latent change score model for Predictor 1

predictor1_T2 ~ 1*predictor1_T1     # This parameter regresses predictor1_T2 perfectly on predictor1_T1
predictor1_T3 ~ 1*predictor1_T2     # This parameter regresses predictor1_T3 perfectly on predictor1_T2
predictor1_T4 ~ 1*predictor1_T3     # This parameter regresses predictor1_T4 perfectly on predictor1_T3

dPred1_1 =~ 1*predictor1_T2       # This defines the change score as measured perfectly by scores on predictor1_T2
dPred1_2 =~ 1*predictor1_T3       # This defines the change score as measured perfectly by scores on predictor1_T3
dPred1_3 =~ 1*predictor1_T4       # This defines the change score as measured perfectly by scores on predictor1_T4

dPred1_1~~dPred1_1 # Estimate variance in change scores
dPred1_2~~dPred1_2
dPred1_3~~dPred1_3

dPred1_1 ~ 1 # Estimate intercept of change scores
dPred1_2 ~ 1
dPred1_3 ~ 1

predictor1_T1~~predictor1_T1 # Only estimate variance of observed Predictor 1 at T1, fix others to zero
predictor1_T2~~0*predictor1_T2
predictor1_T3~~0*predictor1_T3
predictor1_T4~~0*predictor1_T4

predictor1_T1 ~ 1 #Only estimate intercept of observed Predictor 1 at T1, fix others to zero
predictor1_T2 ~ 0*1
predictor1_T3 ~ 0*1
predictor1_T4 ~ 0*1

dPred1_1~predictor1_T1       # This estimates the Predictor 1 self-feedback parameters
dPred1_2~predictor1_T2  + dPred1_1
dPred1_3~predictor1_T3  + dPred1_2

# Latent change score model for Predictor 2

predictor2_T2 ~ 1*predictor2_T1     # This parameter regresses predictor2_T2 perfectly on predictor2_T1
predictor2_T3 ~ 1*predictor2_T2     # This parameter regresses predictor2_T3 perfectly on predictor2_T2
predictor2_T4 ~ 1*predictor2_T3     # This parameter regresses predictor2_T4 perfectly on predictor2_T3

dPred2_1 =~ 1*predictor2_T2       # This defines the change score as measured perfectly by scores on predictor2_T2
dPred2_2 =~ 1*predictor2_T3       # This defines the change score as measured perfectly by scores on predictor2_T3
dPred2_3 =~ 1*predictor2_T4       # This defines the change score as measured perfectly by scores on predictor2_T4

dPred2_1~~dPred2_1 # Estimate variance in change scores
dPred2_2~~dPred2_2
dPred2_3~~dPred2_3

dPred2_1 ~ 1 # Estimate intercept of change scores
dPred2_2 ~ 1
dPred2_3 ~ 1

predictor2_T1~~predictor2_T1 # Only estimate variance of observed Predictor 2 at T1, fix others to zero
predictor2_T2~~0*predictor2_T2
predictor2_T3~~0*predictor2_T3
predictor2_T4~~0*predictor2_T4

predictor2_T1 ~ 1 #Only estimate intercept of observed Predictor 2 at T1, fix others to zero
predictor2_T2 ~ 0*1
predictor2_T3 ~ 0*1
predictor2_T4 ~ 0*1

dPred2_1~predictor2_T1       # # This estimates the Predictor 2 self-feedback parameters
dPred2_2~predictor2_T2  + dPred2_1
dPred2_3~predictor2_T3  + dPred2_2

# Dynamics

dPred1_1~predictor2_T1
dPred1_2~predictor2_T2
dPred1_3~predictor2_T3

dPred2_1~predictor1_T1
dPred2_2~predictor1_T2
dPred2_3~predictor1_T3

predictor2_T1 ~~ predictor1_T1 # Covariance of Pred1 and Pred2 at T1

dPred1_1 ~~   dPred2_1 # Covariances of change scores
dPred1_2 ~~   dPred2_2
dPred1_3 ~~   dPred2_3

# Regression model for Outcome

OutcomeLV =~1*outcome # Outcome is measured by one item, estimate intercept and variance
OutcomeLV ~ 1
OutcomeLV ~~ OutcomeLV
outcome ~~ 0*outcome
# Regress Outcome on Covariate and initial values & change values in Predictor 1 and Predictor 2
OutcomeLV ~  covariate + predictor1_T1 + dPred1_1  + dPred1_2 + dPred1_3  + predictor2_T1 + dPred2_1 + dPred2_2 + dPred2_3
'

Mischa

Are you using the defaults of the blavFitindices function?
How about the median? Remember that these indices are bounded, so might have hit the boundary and with a very skew distribution the mean would be moved to the tail. You can see an example in the help page on how to plot the posterior to see if that is the case

On a more general comment, I dont recommend the RMSEA in general, because it is sensitve to model type/size. I recommend to use CFI and gamma-hat, as these are less sensitive to things like this

Garnier-Villarreal, M., & Jorgensen, T. D. (2020). Adapting Fit Indices for Bayesian Structural Equation Modeling: Comparison to Maximum Likelihood. Psychological Methods, 25(1), 46–70. https://doi.org/dx.doi.org/10.1037/met0000224

Fan, X., & Sivo, S. A. (2007). Sensitivity of fit indices to model misspecification and model types. Multivariate Behavioral Research, 42(3), 509–529. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273170701382864

messages.body_plain:
Ye

When testing measurement invariance with categorical indicators, you should test for threslholds first, then test for loadings, and then intercepts. This way the threshold model defines a first order measurement model between the categorical answers and the underlying factor

See

Wu, H., & Estabrook, R. (2016). Identification of confirmatory factor analysis models of different levels of invariance for ordered categorical outcomes. Psychometrika, 81(4), 1014–1045. doi: 10.1007/s11336-016-9506-0

When you say that it doesnt converged, what do you mean? After how many iterations? How high is the R-hat? When you add the wiggle it commonly needs more iterations

Sorry I cant read the code in detail now

On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 5:18:14 AM UTC+2 Ye wrote:
> Hi Dr. Garnier-Villarreal and Dr.Merkle,

> Thank you very much for your help with my previous questions!
>
> I encountered more issues while testing the approximate invariance with ordered categorical items.
>
> To reduce the computation time, I treated the longitudinal measurement invariance test question as a multi-group one and converted the data into a long format. I used the Lavan default method for model identification and the models converged with the WLSMV estimator. Specifically,
>
> 1. Configural model: freely estimates loadings and thresholds in all groups, and constrains the latent item responses as variances of 1 and intercepts of 0 in all groups. The common-factor variances are set to 1 and means are set to 0 in all groups.
> 2. Loadings invariance model: constrained the loadings to be equal across groups, thresholds freely estimated in all groups. The latent item responses were constrained with variances of 1 and intercepts of 0. The common-factor variances were constrained to 1 in the first group and freely estimated in other groups, and the common-factor means were constrained to 0 in all groups.
> 3. Thresholds invariance model: constrained the loadings and thresholds to be equal across groups. The latent item variances were fixed to 1 in the first group and freely estimated in other groups. The common-factor mean and variance were fixed to 0 and 1 in the first group and freely estimated in other groups.
>
> To test loading approximate invariance, I added the labels of item loadings in the wiggle statement, and the models converged with different data I simulated.
> However, when I further tested the loading exact invariance + thresholds, approximate invariance model, by adding the thresholds labels into the wiggle statements, the models failed to converge.
> Similarly, when testing the loadings + thresholds approximate invariance model, the models failed to converge. Moreover, some of the models had an error message: Error in validate_ll(x) : All input values must be finite.
>
> I understand that treating longitudinal data as multi-group data introduces a definite source of model misspecification that may cause the convergence issue. However, I tried testing the thresholds approximate invariance model using the wide format data, but I still have the convergence issue with the thresholds approximate invariance model and loading + thresholds approximate invariance model.
>
> Do you have any suggestions on correctly testing the thresholds approximate invariance with ordered categorical indicators? e.g. specific model identification methods, increase the burin-in sample, or increase/decrease the wiggle sd?

messages.body_plain:
Ye,

I tried a short run of bfit.scalar (100 burnin/100 sample) and got convergence. I suspect the problem could be related to std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE paired with uninformative priors on loadings. You might consider more informative priors on the loadings. For example, if all items are known to be in the same direction, you might use something like normal(1, .33) there. I generally think that normal(0, big SD) is not best for loadings, because people almost always know the intended direction of the items.

Also, for groups 2-4, the variance of each observed variable is free. These priors default to gamma(1,.5) (on SD, not variance), which again might be too uninformative and combine with loadings to cause problems. Because the SDs are fixed to 1 in group 1, I would opt for priors that place more density around 1, like maybe

dp = dpriors(lambda = "normal(1,.33)", theta = "gamma(4,4)[sd]")

Also, for the wiggle argument, you can shorten it to something like

wiggle = c("loadings", "thresholds")

Hope it helps,
Ed

> > > > Are you using the defaults of the blavFitindices function?
> > > > How about the median? Remember that these indices are bounded, so might have hit the boundary and with a very skew distribution the mean would be moved to the tail. You can see an example in the help page on how to plot the posterior to see if that is the case

messages.body_plain:
Mischa

I just remember another post here, that had a similar issue. When the ML model has low df, this happended.

So, what happens is that RMSEA is a measure of misfit per df. The new method corrects the estimated deviation by the effective number of parameters (pD), and with few df, loo/waic over corrects it in comparosin to the ML models. These differences between pD is not much, and in most common scenarios (larger models) dic is gives the wrong "correction". But in these specific scenarios and just for RMSEA loo/waic corrects more than expected

Hope this helps

Once more thank you for your explaining!
So, it would be appropriate to argue that using DIC is the better, more correct option in this context (because loo/waic over-correct the pDs) ? Because I want to avoid simply choosing the option that gives the more convenient estimate.

> Mischa
>
> I just remember another post here, that had a similar issue. When the ML model has low df, this happended.
>
> So, what happens is that RMSEA is a measure of misfit per df. The new method corrects the estimated deviation by the effective number of parameters (pD), and with few df, loo/waic over corrects it in comparosin to the ML models. These differences between pD is not much, and in most common scenarios (larger models) dic is gives the wrong "correction". But in these specific scenarios and just for RMSEA loo/waic corrects more than expected

> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > However, in my model, I have noticed that the estimated (posterior mean) BRMSEA is quite different from the maximum likelihood estimate (.15 instead of .07). This is specific to the BRMSEA and not the same for, eg. BCFI, - there, results are very similiar to the frequentist estimates.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > When trying out different models using other data, it also seemed that the BRMSEA is especially sensitive.
> > > > > > > > > How should one deal with such results? I know that the overall posterior is more important than the mean, but for the BRMSEA it seems like the entire distribution is very far from the ML point estimate. Is it because of the type of model used (df=16, N=350)?
> > > > > > > > > Any help or ideas are greatly appreciated!

messages.body_plain:
"better" is loaded term. Maybe is better to have the loo pD, and is the actual "truest" correction?

You can argue, that to be the most similar to ML fit indices, in cases with few df, DIC pD is the best approximation for RMSEA (as the other fit indices are not affected)

> Once more thank you for your explaining!
> So, it would be appropriate to argue that using DIC is the better, more correct option in this context (because loo/waic over-correct the pDs) ? Because I want to avoid simply choosing the option that gives the more convenient estimate.
>
> mauga...@gmail.com schrieb am Mittwoch, 24. August 2022 um 21:53:41 UTC+2:
> > Mischa
> >
> > I just remember another post here, that had a similar issue. When the ML model has low df, this happended.
> >
> > So, what happens is that RMSEA is a measure of misfit per df. The new method corrects the estimated deviation by the effective number of parameters (pD), and with few df, loo/waic over corrects it in comparosin to the ML models. These differences between pD is not much, and in most common scenarios (larger models) dic is gives the wrong "correction". But in these specific scenarios and just for RMSEA loo/waic corrects more than expected

messages.body_plain:
Mischa, Mauricio,

This issue seems a little tricky to me because the best answer might be "more research is needed to decide about loo vs dic". In general, I think that loo is to be trusted more than dic for assessing effective number of parameters.

It might also be that the traditional rmsea cutoffs do not work well here... this recent paper (not Bayesian) talks about cutoffs that are adapted to your specific model, which might also be interesting for Bayesian metrics:

https://psyarxiv.com/v8yru/

Also, here is published work on the behavior of rmsea with small df (in a non-Bayesian context):

https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00273171.2020.1868965

On Thu, 2022-08-25 at 01:06 -0700, 'Mischa vk' via blavaan wrote:
> Once more thank you for your explaining!
> So, it would be appropriate to argue that using DIC is the better, more correct option in this context (because loo/waic over-correct the pDs) ? Because I want to avoid simply choosing the option that gives the more convenient estimate.
>
> mauga...@gmail.com schrieb am Mittwoch, 24. August 2022 um 21:53:41 UTC+2:
> > Mischa
> >
> > I just remember another post here, that had a similar issue. When the ML model has low df, this happended.
> >
> > So, what happens is that RMSEA is a measure of misfit per df. The new method corrects the estimated deviation by the effective number of parameters (pD), and with few df, loo/waic over corrects it in comparosin to the ML models. These differences between pD is not much, and in most common scenarios (larger models) dic is gives the wrong "correction". But in these specific scenarios and just for RMSEA loo/waic corrects more than expected
> >
> > Hope this helps

messages.body_plain:
Ed and Mischa

I dont think we need more research. Because research has shown consistently that RMSEA is not a great fit index, basically guided by model type and size (df), same conclusion as the one you shared here.

Thats why for overall model fit I recommend SRMR, CFI, and gamma-hat

The idea of model specify cutoffs is interesting, several people have suggested it over time. One of the main reasons to develop the simsem R package, does this very easily. But it leads to similar issues as power analysis. Now you have to define popolation paraemters for the model, and "acceptable misfit" of the model. Whcih can take many forms, and hard to decide in applied reasearch

On Thursday, August 25, 2022 at 4:13:25 PM UTC+2 Ed Merkle wrote:
> Mischa, Mauricio,
>

> Also, here is published work on the behavior of rmsea with small df (in a non-Bayesian context):

> > > So, what happens is that RMSEA is a measure of misfit per df. The new method corrects the estimated deviation by the effective number of parameters (pD), and with few df, loo/waic over corrects it in comparosin to the ML models. These differences between pD is not much, and in most common scenarios (larger models) dic is gives the wrong "correction". Ed and Mischa

messages.subject: Re: Longitudinal Measurement Invariance
messages.subject_clean: Longitudinal Measurement Invariance
messages.body_plain:
Thank you Dr. Garnier-Villarreal and Dr.Merkle for your suggestions! They are really helpful.

I am running the models with simulated data, including both the non-invariant populations and variant populations. I recorded the number of models that had a maximum R hat larger than 1.1, with 1000 burnin and 1000 sample. Based on the results I have so far, nearly all of the exact loading + thresholds approximate invariance model and loading + thresholds approximate invariance models had a maximum R-hat larger than 1.1, across conditions and replications.

Unfortunately, I only recorded the model fit indices so it is difficult to trace back to the largest R-hat of the non-converged models. I do get the warning messages ' The largest R-hat is 2.33, indicating chains have not mixed.' and 'blavaan WARNING: Small effective sample sizes (< 100) for some parameters.'

I tried adding informative priors to an example data that reported issues before, and it helped! I would incorporate it into the codes and increase the iterations sample in my further simulations. As a follow-up question, the error message: "Error in validate_ll(x) : All input values must be finite." is also caused by model non-convergence, right?

Besides, I tried following the Wu & Estabrook approach to testing thresholds invariance, the df of the baseline model and threshold invariance model is the same. Does that suggest the thresholds invariance model of three-ordered categoricals is not testable? If so, is the current identification approach (lavvan default) the right way to go or is it not recommended?

Thank you again for all your help!

Best regards,
Ye

On Tuesday, August 23, 2022 at 11:57:27 AM UTC-4 Ed Merkle wrote:
> Ye,
>
> I tried a short run of bfit.scalar (100 burnin/100 sample) and got convergence. I suspect the problem could be related to std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE paired with uninformative priors on loadings. You might consider more informative priors on the loadings. For example, if all items are known to be in the same direction, you might use something like normal(1, .33) there. I generally think that normal(0, big SD) is not best for loadings, because people almost always know the intended direction of the items.
>
> Also, for groups 2-4, the variance of each observed variable is free. These priors default to gamma(1,.5) (on SD, not variance), which again might be too uninformative and combine with loadings to cause problems. Because the SDs are fixed to 1 in group 1, I would opt for priors that place more density around 1, like maybe
>
> dp = dpriors(lambda = "normal(1,.33)", theta = "gamma(4,4)[sd]")
>
> Also, for the wiggle argument, you can shorten it to something like
>
> wiggle = c("loadings", "thresholds")
>
> Hope it helps,
> Ed
>
>
>
> On Mon, 2022-08-22 at 20:18 -0700, Ye wrote:
> > Hi Dr. Garnier-Villarreal and Dr.Merkle,
> >
> > Thank you very much for your help with my previous questions!
> >
> > I encountered more issues while testing the approximate invariance with ordered categorical items.
> >
> > To reduce the computation time, I treated the longitudinal measurement invariance test question as a multi-group one and converted the data into a long format. I used the Lavan default method for model identification and the models converged with the WLSMV estimator. Specifically,
> >
> > 1. Configural model: freely estimates loadings and thresholds in all groups, and constrains the latent item responses as variances of 1 and intercepts of 0 in all groups. The common-factor variances are set to 1 and means are set to 0 in all groups.
> > 2. Loadings invariance model: constrained the loadings to be equal across groups, thresholds freely estimated in all groups. The latent item responses were constrained with variances of 1 and intercepts of 0. The common-factor variances were constrained to 1 in the first group and freely estimated in other groups, and the common-factor means were constrained to 0 in all groups.
> > 3. Thresholds invariance model: constrained the loadings and thresholds to be equal across groups. The latent item variances were fixed to 1 in the first group and freely estimated in other groups. The common-factor mean and variance were fixed to 0 and 1 in the first group and freely estimated in other groups.
> >
> > To test loading approximate invariance, I added the labels of item loadings in the wiggle statement, and the models converged with different data I simulated.
> > However, when I further tested the loading exact invariance + thresholds, approximate invariance model, by adding the thresholds labels into the wiggle statements, the models failed to converge.
> > Similarly, when testing the loadings + thresholds approximate invariance model, the models failed to converge. Moreover, some of the models had an error message: Error in validate_ll(x) : All input values must be finite.
> >
> > I understand that treating longitudinal data as multi-group data introduces a definite source of model misspecification that may cause the convergence issue. However, I tried testing the thresholds approximate invariance model using the wide format data, but I still have the convergence issue with the thresholds approximate invariance model and loading + thresholds approximate invariance model.
> >
> > Do you have any suggestions on correctly testing the thresholds approximate invariance with ordered categorical indicators? e.g. specific model identification methods, increase the burin-in sample, or increase/decrease the wiggle sd?
> >
> >  I attached the syntax and data for your reference. Thank you very much!

messages.body_plain:
Ye

When you fix the threshold model you whould not have the same df.

In the configural model you have "theta" parameterization, nothing is fixed equal between groups/time points
Threshold model: fix thresholds equall between groups/time points. Freely estimate the intercepts and variances of the indicators of group 2 (keep fixed the ones for group 1).

My guess is that you fixed the thresholds, but didnt fee the intercepts and variances

Look at this quick example from the semTools package

library(semTools)

?measEq.syntax

mod.cat <http://mod.cat> <- ' FU1 =~ u1 + u2 + u3 + u4'

syntax.config <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mod.cat <http://mod.cat>, data = datCat,
                               ordered = paste0("u", 1:4),
                               parameterization = "theta",
                               ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                               group = "g")

mod.config <- as.character(syntax.config)
fit.config <- cfa(mod.config, data = datCat, group = "g",
                  ordered = paste0("u", 1:4), parameterization = "theta")
summary(fit.config)

## metric invariance
syntax.thr <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mod.cat <http://mod.cat>, data = datCat,
                               ordered = paste0("u", 1:4),
                               parameterization = "theta",
                               ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                               group = "g",
                               group.equal = c("thresholds"))
summary(syntax.thr)                    # summarize model features
mod.thr <- as.character(syntax.thr) # save as text
cat(mod.thr)

fit.thr <- cfa(mod.thr, data = datCat, group = "g",
                  ordered = paste0("u", 1:4), parameterization = "theta")
summary(fit.thr)

anova(fit.config, fit.thr)
